newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian military satellite launch in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Russian military satellite launch in doubt.

text.p: Local authorities in Russia's remote Yakutia region urged Moscow on Saturday to cancel a military satellite launch because of fears for the environment, Itar-Tass news agency said

In a potential new setback for Russia's space programme, Tass said officials in Yakutia, a vast, sparsely inhabited region of eastern and northeastern Russia, were concerned by the possible damage when stages of a Start-1 booster rocket fall to earth after Tuesday's launch from Russia's Far East.

Tass said Yakutia government officials had sent a letter to the defence ministry threatening to pull out of a 1996 agreement, which allows booster rocket stages to fall on their territory, if the launch goes ahead without their consent.

"We doubt the environmental and technical safety of the rocket, and Russia's military space forces are unable to present materials that documentarily refute our apprehension," Tass quoted Yakutia deputy prime minister Yegor Borisov as saying.
Officials from the Svobodny space centre which will launch the Zeya satellite visited Yakutia's main city of Yakutsk, about 4,000 km (2,500 miles) east of Moscow, three days ago.
But their efforts to persuade the local authorities that there was no threat to the environment clearly failed.
The defence ministry in Moscow was not immediately able to comment.
The row threatened to dampen celebrations of the first anniversary of President Boris Yeltsin's decision on March 1, 1996, to award Svobodny official status as a space centre.
The space industry, once the pride of the Soviet Union, has fallen on hard times since the superpower collapsed in 1991.
Cash problems have caused delays in Russia's work under a project to build an international space station called Alpha and have delayed several launches in recent years.
A fire last month on the ageing Russian orbital station Mir, while an American and a German were on board, did little to bolster global confidence in Moscow's space programme.

Russia's commercial satellite programme is one of the few bright spots. The Khrunichev Space Centre said last Tuesday it planned to make eight Proton rocket launches in 1997, sending a total of 20 Western satellites into orbit.
